extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, patent examiners, and IP counsel (Korean patent litigation context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards used by the Korean Patent Court for evaluating patentability issues (inventiveness/obviousness, enablement/description, first-to-file, product-by-process, procedural standing) in invalidation and infringement proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness / obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventiveness is judged according to whether the invention could have been easily conceived by a person of ordinary skill in the art from the prior art technologies on the basis of the objective, constitution, and effect of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment examines whether claimed features are derivable from cited references (alone or in combination), whether the combination would have been easy for a person skilled in the art, and whether prior art disclosures and motivations make the claimed solution obvious. Consider objective, constitution, and effect of the invention as the baseline for the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical common sense and selection of known methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a suitable method or changing a disclosed structure can be a matter of technical common sense to a person of ordinary skill in the art when the specification or prior art suggests such alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cited reference's specification suggests that a component's structure can be changed and alternative methods (e.g., flowing-type vs immersion-type) were publicly known, replacing one method with another may be unremarkable. Development trends (e.g., miniaturization, efficiency) can provide motivation to make such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A replacement or combination of an element from one cited reference with an element from another is supported when prior art suggests benefits (e.g., reduce device volume, reduce time) and there is no particular technical difficulty in making the replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for sufficient motivation in the prior art (e.g., explicit disclosures of advantages) and absence of technical difficulty; if an element of a cited reference includes all constitutional elements of a claim and prior art suggests benefits, combination to reach the claim can be considered obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as a secondary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success of a product embodying the claimed invention is only one reference material and does not by itself prove inventiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventiveness should be judged primarily on whether the invention could have been easily conceived from prior art technologies (objective, constitution, effect). Commercial success cannot override an otherwise obvious finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional equivalence / same technical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Different descriptive terms in prior art (e.g., 'rough surface', 'concave and convex portions', 'inter-granular cracks') may have the same technical meaning if they share the same technical characteristics and effects (such as increasing surface area and wettability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two disclosures produce the same technical effect and are based on the same principle, they can be treated as equivalent for inventive-step analysis. Demonstrating that prior art discloses the same technical characteristics (and effects) undermines novelty/inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher expectation-of-success threshold for certain medicinal inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For cancer therapeutic (and similar difficult biomedical) medicinal-use inventions, inventiveness can be denied over the prior art only when a person of ordinary skill in the art could have reasonably expected the success of discovering the medicinal use from the prior art (a higher bar than mere possibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of unpredictability in biological systems, complexity of causes (e.g., gene mutations), and high development costs/time, the court requires a reasonable expectation of success (not just a prospect or possibility) in order to deny inventiveness for such inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance required for numerical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed numerical limitation (e.g., a concentration threshold) must have a recognized critical significance or show a remarkable effect within vs outside the claimed range to support inventiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim differs from prior art only by a numerical range, the specification must provide grounds, rationale, embodiments, or evidence showing a remarkable difference in effect tied to that numerical limit; absent such grounds, the numerical limitation alone is insufficient to establish inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process vs product claim inventive test
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim (defining a product by how it is made) may lack inventiveness if the completed product has no difference in structure or effect from a prior-art product; conversely, a process (manufacturing) claim can be inventive if the process feature is non-obvious and yields a distinguishable or remarkable effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the completed product's structure/effect compared to prior art — if identical, product-by-process claim may fail. For process claims, determine whether the claimed process step(s) (e.g., 'fixing an ion exchange film to flow frames before stacking') could be easily derived and whether they produce a notable technical advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file identity test (Article 36(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an earlier-filed cited reference claim includes all the features of a later-filed claim and only adds an additional feature, and that additional feature is not an essential basic element, the earlier (narrower) claim can be deemed identical to the later (broader) claim, making the later-filed claim unpatentable under the first-to-file rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether common features can be separated from the additional feature and whether the additional feature is essential to the invention; if not essential and the earlier claim covers the common features, treat the inventions as identical for first-to-file purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification description requirements for Markush-type claims (Article 42(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush-type medicinal claim does not violate description requirements merely because some selective elements are not described as specific embodiments in the specification, provided a person of ordinary skill could understand and practice the effect of the invention from the specification and such effect can be fully expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on enablement and sufficiency: if the spec allows the skilled person to carry out the invention and reasonably expect the claimed effect, missing specific embodiments of each Markush option do not automatically render the claim deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of applicable prior art across industrial fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited references from different industrial fields can be adopted to deny inventiveness when the technical features of those references are not limited to a specific field and a person of ordinary skill in the subject field could apply them without particular difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the objectives, technical problems, and features of the inventions overall. If the technical element is widely applicable or addresses the same objective across fields, it is reasonable to rely on such prior art rather than restrict prior art to the exact industrial field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denied obviousness when combination requires abandoning core means
rubrics_metrics.description: Ease in combining cited references is denied if deriving the claimed invention would require substantially modifying the structure of a cited reference to the extent of abandoning the means by which that reference solves its problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If combining a 'well-known' technology with a reference would destroy the core solution or create structural interference (e.g., wedge-inserting devices interfering with each other), the combination is not a straightforward derivation and obviousness may be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural standing / negative scope confirmation interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative scope confirmation action (brought to confirm a right not to be infringed) filed immediately after a defendant expects an unfavorable decision in an infringement action may be held to have no interest in confirmation and thus be dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider factors such as litigation economy, absence of remaining insecurity or legal risk to be removed, undue burden on the patentee, separation of judicial and administrative powers, and the risk of contradictory judgments when deciding whether to accept such confirmation actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of use requiring structural change can defeat obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed device differs in use (and corresponding structure/strength/size) from the cited reference, shifting the use in an obviousness combination may not be feasible if it requires accompanying changes in the entire structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deriving the claimed invention from a cited reference would necessitate substantial structural alterations tied to a different use (e.g., converting a cosmetic bottle to a chiropractic massager), a person of ordinary skill would not easily conceive that change and inventiveness may be upheld.
